rubric.why: Identifies van der Waals forces as weak attractions between molecules.
rubric.description: States that these are weak intermolecular forces or attractions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing them as weak attractions between molecules.

rubric.why: Mentions the dipoles associated with these attractions.
rubric.description: Connects the forces with temporary or induced dipoles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning temporary, instantaneous, or induced dipoles.

modelAnswer: Van der Waals forces are weak attractive forces between molecules.
They arise due to temporary or induced dipoles in the molecules.

items.followUp: Define a suspension and give one example.

rubric.why: A colloid consists of particles of one substance dispersed through another.
rubric.description: Describes a colloid as particles of one substance dispersed in another.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the dispersed particles.

rubric.why: A suitable example completes the definition question.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a colloid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any correct example, such as milk, fog, or paint.

modelAnswer: A colloidal solution is a heterogeneous mixture in which very small particles of one substance are dispersed throughout another substance and do not settle on standing.
Example: milk.

items.followUp: A solution contains 12 g of solute in 60 g of solution. Calculate its mass percentage.

rubric.why: Mass percentage is based on the mass of solute relative to the total mass of solution.
rubric.description: Gives the ratio of mass of solute to mass of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ratio.

rubric.why: The ratio is multiplied by 100 to express it as a percentage.
rubric.description: States that the ratio is multiplied by 100.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including multiplication by 100.

modelAnswer: Mass percentage = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100.
It is the mass of solute present in 100 parts by mass of solution.

items.followUp: Name two factors that affect the rate at which a solid solute dissolves.

rubric.why: Temperature, pressure, and the nature of the substances are factors affecting solubility.
rubric.description: Names one valid factor affecting solubility.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one of temperature, pressure, or the nature of the solute or solvent.

rubric.why: The question asks for two different factors.
rubric.description: Names a second valid factor affecting solubility.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second distinct factor from the listed alternatives.

modelAnswer: Two factors that affect the solubility of solutes are temperature and the nature of the solute and solvent.

items.followUp: Why does atomic size generally decrease from left to right across a period?

rubric.why: Across a period, the nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same shell.
rubric.description: States that nuclear charge or effective nuclear charge increases across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the increase in nuclear charge.

rubric.why: The stronger attraction makes electron loss more difficult and reduces electropositive character.
rubric.description: Links the increased attraction to greater difficulty in losing electrons or decreased electropositive character.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct consequence.

modelAnswer: Across a period, the nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell.
The outer electrons are attracted more strongly, so atoms lose electrons less readily and electropositive character decreases.

items.followUp: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of magnesium with oxygen.

rubric.why: Group 2 elements react with oxygen to form oxides.
rubric.description: Identifies the product as an oxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that oxides are formed.

rubric.why: A general or specific balanced equation illustrates the reaction.
rubric.description: Gives a balanced equation for a Group 2 element reacting with oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct balanced equation, such as 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

modelAnswer: Group 2 elements react with oxygen to form metal oxides.
General equation: 2M + O₂ → 2MO.

items.followUp: State two physical properties of metals.

rubric.why: Non-metals have characteristic physical properties such as brittleness and poor conductivity.
rubric.description: Gives one correct physical property of non-metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct property.

rubric.why: The question asks for physical properties in the plural.
rubric.description: Gives another correct physical property of non-metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second distinct correct property.

modelAnswer: Non-metals are generally dull and do not have metallic lustre.
When solid, they are usually brittle and are neither malleable nor ductile.
They are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.
They are usually not sonorous and often have low densities and low melting and boiling points.

items.followUp: Define an atom and classify elements as monoatomic, diatomic, triatomic, or polyatomic with one example of each.

rubric.why: A molecule is defined by its ability to exist independently and retain the properties of the substance.
rubric.description: Defines a molecule as the smallest particle capable of independent existence and retaining the substance's properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the essential definition.

rubric.why: A monoatomic molecule contains one atom.
rubric.description: Explains the monoatomic type and gives or implies a correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for monoatomic = one atom, with an example such as He, Ar, or Ne.

rubric.why: A diatomic molecule contains two atoms.
rubric.description: Explains the diatomic type and gives or implies a correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for diatomic = two atoms, with an example such as H₂, O₂, or N₂.

rubric.why: A triatomic molecule contains three atoms.
rubric.description: Explains the triatomic type and gives or implies a correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for triatomic = three atoms, with an example such as O₃, CO₂, or H₂O.

rubric.why: A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms.
rubric.description: Explains the polyatomic type and gives or implies a correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for polyatomic = more than three atoms, with an example such as P₄ or S₈.

modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance capable of independent existence and retaining the chemical properties of that substance.
Monoatomic molecules contain one atom; example: helium (He).
Diatomic molecules contain two atoms; example: oxygen (O₂).
Triatomic molecules contain three atoms; example: ozone (O₃).
Polyatomic molecules contain more than three atoms; example: phosphorus (P₄).
